items.title: Bartlett made the first noble gas compound in 1962
items.claim: Until 1962 every chemistry textbook said noble gases were entirely unreactive. Neil Bartlett at UBC noticed that O2's ionisation energy (1175 kJ/mol) almost matches xenon's (1170). PtF6 had stripped an electron from O2. So PtF6 should be able to oxidise xenon. He tried it. XePtF6 formed instantly.
items.prompt: Why did this single result change inorganic chemistry?

options.text: It broke the assumed inviolability of the noble-gas 'rule of full octets' and opened the chemistry of an entire group of elements that had been written off as inert

items.reveal:
Bartlett's noticed PtF6 (a deep red solid) turned air red on contact: PtF6 had oxidised O2 to O2+ PtF6-. He looked up xenon's ionisation energy, saw the near-equality with O2, and reasoned that PtF6 should also oxidise xenon.

The synthesis (Vancouver, March 1962) used a gas-handling apparatus he had built himself. Within months, Claassen, Selig and Malm at Argonne produced XeF4 by simply heating xenon with fluorine at 400°C.

Today: XeF2, XeF4, XeF6, XeO3, XeO4, KrF2, ArF (the last only at cryogenic temperatures). Bartlett died in 2008. His insight made the chemistry of noble gases a real subject overnight.
items.why: Chemistry has 'laws' that turn out to be untested generalisations. A single decisive experiment can break a 70-year consensus.

items.title: Lavoisier overthrew phlogiston with a balance, then was guillotined
items.claim: By careful mass measurements in sealed vessels, Antoine Lavoisier showed that combustion is the combination of substances with oxygen, not the release of phlogiston. He renamed oxygen, defined elements as substances chemistry cannot break down, and was executed during the French Revolution in 1794.

options.text: Quantitative measurement — burning metals GAIN weight; phlogiston theory had no explanation for that, while Lavoisier's oxygen theory predicted exactly how much weight should be gained

items.reveal:
Lavoisier published his Traité Élémentaire de Chimie in 1789 — the first modern chemistry textbook. He listed 33 'elements' (some, like caloric and light, were later removed), defined elements as substances that could not be further decomposed, and insisted chemistry must be a quantitative science centred on mass balance.

He was a tax collector for the ancien régime (the Ferme Générale, profitable and loathed). On 8 May 1794 he was guillotined at age 50. Lagrange remarked: 'It took only an instant to cut off that head, and a hundred years may not produce another like it.'

His wife Marie-Anne Paulze translated his work, illustrated his books, and after his death edited and published his last memoirs.
items.why: Scientific revolutions can be driven by precise measurement rather than dramatic new observations. The balance reorganised chemistry.

items.title: Gases mix even when nothing energetic is gained
items.claim: Open a perfume bottle in still air. The fragrance fills the room. There is essentially zero enthalpy change — no heat is released. Yet the mixing is utterly spontaneous and would NEVER reverse on its own.
items.prompt: What drives mixing with no energy reward?

options.text: Entropy of mixing: vastly more microstates have the perfume molecules spread through the room than concentrated near the bottle; the system follows the overwhelming statistical odds

items.reveal:
For two ideal gases mixing at constant T and P, ΔH ≈ 0. But ΔS = -nR(x1 ln x1 + x2 ln x2), always positive when x1 and x2 are both non-zero. Gibbs free energy ΔG = ΔH - TΔS is therefore negative, and mixing is spontaneous.

The perfume could in principle un-mix into the bottle. The probability is roughly 1 in 10 to the (10 to the 23) — for practical purposes, zero. The second law is a statistical statement, not an absolute prohibition.

This logic underpins every observation that systems 'tend to disorder': cards left in a deck, gases filling containers, hot bodies cooling. Pure entropy with no enthalpy change is enough to drive the process firmly forward.
items.why: Spontaneity is often taught as 'releases energy'. Pure entropy of mixing — with no heat — drives transformations all by itself.
